idiom_name: sealed interface + record variants + exhaustive switch expression
implementation_notes: Java 17 and later close the set with a sealed interface (or sealed abstract class): only the types listed in permits may implement it, records are implicitly final, and the combination is what JEP 409 calls algebraic data types - records for the products, sealed types for the sum. A switch expression over a sealed type is checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler (standard from Java 21, preview from 17), so no default arm is needed and a new variant is a compile error at every switch. Keep the variants in the same package or module, and use private records or a package-private constructor for the members that must not be constructed outside the model.
pitfalls: A permitted subtype declared non-sealed reopens the hierarchy for that branch, and the compiler then requires a default arm - the guarantee is lost exactly where it was needed.

Reflection, frameworks and serializers can still fabricate instances (Unsafe, Jackson creator bypass): the closed set constrains the source, not every byte that reaches the JVM memory, so validate at deserialization.
Records are shallowly immutable: a record component of type List stays mutable, so the legal-shape guarantee must be completed by defensive copies in the canonical constructor.

variants.name: Pre-sealed closed hierarchy consumed by a Visitor
variants.idiom_name: package-private base constructor + final variants + Visitor<R>
variants.implementation_notes: Before sealed types, Java expressed the pattern with a base class whose only constructor is package-private (so no class outside the package can extend it) and one final variant per state, consumed through a Visitor interface with one method per variant - adding a state breaks every visitor implementation at compile time, which is the closest the language offered to exhaustiveness. Choose this variant in codebases pinned below Java 17 or in APIs that must expose the model to Java 8 callers; the closure and the exhaustiveness are conventions plus the visitor interface rather than compiler-enforced properties, so the model has to stay in one package and reviewers must guard the base constructor.
pitfalls: The base constructor is only package-private, not sealed: one class in the same package (or a reflective call to setAccessible) can add a variant and no other module is told.
Visitor implementations that return null or throw from the default case defeat the exhaustiveness the pattern buys; every method must be implemented even if it only reports an error.
Nested or anonymous subclasses created in tests can quietly become part of the hierarchy - keep the variants in one compilation unit and test through the public factories.
